title: The Conversion of Saint Paul (25 January)
hookLine: the unity week ends with the Damascus road

cards: Look at the well-known paintings of this scene, Caravaggio's for one, and you'll see a man flat on his back in the dirt, arms thrown up, and a huge horse standing over him.
It's the picture that stuck: Paul knocked off his horse. But Acts never mentions a horse, not once in the three times the story is told. The artists added it.
What Acts does give us is stranger than a fall from a saddle, and the unity week ends on it.

teach.b: Saul of Tarsus was a Pharisee, zealous for his tradition and certain that the followers of Jesus were a danger to it. He had stood by at Stephen's death.
Now he carries letters from the high priest to arrest followers of the Way in Damascus. Near the city, a light from heaven flashes around him. He falls to the ground and hears a voice.
In the Douay-Rheims: "Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?" Not my followers. Me.
Saul asks, "Who art thou, Lord?" And the answer: "I am Jesus whom thou persecutest."
Some readers hear in that word a seed of what Paul would later write: the Church as the body of Christ, so what is done to its members is done to him.
Saul gets up blind. His companions lead him by the hand into the city, the hunter now helpless, and for three days he neither eats nor drinks.
Then the Lord sends a disciple named Ananias, who objects: he has heard how much harm this man has done, and why he has come. He goes anyway, lays hands on him, and calls him brother Saul.

teach.h: I AM JESUS WHOM THOU PERSECUTEST.
teach.b: Something like scales fall from Saul's eyes, and he is baptized. One more correction: the conversion doesn't rename him.
Acts keeps calling him Saul for several more chapters; only later, on his travels, does it say Saul, who is also called Paul.
His conversion has its own feast, and it closes the unity week: the man who set out to break up the community spends the rest of Acts building it.

how: Catholics keep January 25 as the feast of the Conversion of Saint Paul, which also closes the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity, often with an ecumenical Vespers in Rome at the Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls.

games.q: you're Ananias. the Lord tells you to go and lay hands on Saul, the man who came to arrest you. what do you do?
o: object, then go and call him brother.
send someone else in your place.
games.why: Ananias objects, he has heard what this man has done, but goes, lays hands on him and says, brother Saul.

practice: Bring to mind someone headed the wrong way, an angry relative, a friend in trouble, a public figure who frightens you, and instead of rehearsing what they've done, picture them on a road with a light reaching them.
Then think of Ananias, who had to go and call his enemy brother. If you pray, pray for that person to turn and for yourself to be ready when they do; if not, simply wish them a road back.

wordCard.voice: Ananias, the disciple. Sent to the blinded Saul in Damascus, frightened but obedient, the one who called him brother and healed his eyes. Today's word.
